title: The big picture
dek: The background that makes the rest of Karnak make sense: how the temple grew, who built it, which gods lived here, how it was built and what happened to it.

growth.intro: Drag the slider or step through. Each step shows what was built (outlined) and what was pulled down (dashed). Tap any building for details.

steps.label: Senusret I
steps.text: The story starts with a limestone temple for Amun-Ra built by Senusret I, probably on the site of smaller earlier shrines. It had a pillared porch with statues of the king as Osiris, and an inner room where Amun’s statue stood in a shrine on a calcite stand. The king’s White Chapel stood somewhere outside it.

steps.label: Amenhotep I
steps.text: The first kings of the New Kingdom started adding in front of the old temple. Amenhotep I lined its forecourt with chapels and storerooms, set up a calcite shrine for the god’s boat, and built a gateway at the west door.

steps.label: Thutmose I
steps.text: Thutmose I gave the temple its first stone gateways that still stand: the Fourth and Fifth Pylons, with stone walls round the core. Between them he built a hall for statues of himself as Osiris, and in front of the Fourth Pylon, then the main entrance, he set up two granite obelisks.

steps.label: Thutmose II
steps.text: Thutmose II pushed the front further west with a new pylon, creating a deep festival court around his father’s obelisks. This pylon was later pulled down, so it has no number in today’s system.

steps.label: Hatshepsut
steps.text: Hatshepsut rebuilt the heart of the temple. She cleared Amenhotep I’s shrine and gateway, built a suite of rooms round the sanctuary (the “Palace of Maat”) with her quartzite Red Chapel for the god’s [[bark|boat]], and raised obelisks: a pair in her father’s hall, a pair for Thutmose II and a pair at the east end. To the south she built the Eighth Pylon, on the route towards the temples of Mut and Luxor.

steps.label: Thutmose III
steps.text: Thutmose III changed the plan most. Behind the old temple he added a whole new temple, the Akhmenu, and walled it in. He added the Sixth Pylon, the Seventh Pylon on the southern route, a small temple on the east wall for people who could not go inside, and the Sacred Lake. He also took down Hatshepsut’s Red Chapel and replaced it with a granite shrine, and swapped Amenhotep I’s crumbling limestone chapels for sandstone ones.

steps.label: Amenhotep III
steps.text: Amenhotep III tore down the whole festival court in front of the Fourth Pylon, with the pylon of Thutmose II and the chapels that stood there (among them the White Chapel and the Red Chapel blocks), and used them as fill for his new Third Pylon. He also began the Tenth Pylon in the south, but stopped after a few courses.

steps.label: Akhenaten
steps.text: His son started as Amenhotep IV and built huge temples for the sun disk, the Aten, just east of Karnak, from small standard blocks called [[talatat]]. Then he changed his name to Akhenaten, attacked Amun, had his name and figure cut out of the walls, and left Thebes. The temple was closed.

steps.label: Horemheb
steps.text: After Tutankhamun reopened the temples, Horemheb had Akhenaten’s buildings taken apart block by block and packed them into his own new pylons: the Second Pylon (the new front of the temple), the Ninth, and the Tenth, which he finished.

steps.label: Sety I and Ramesses II
steps.text: Sety I filled the open space between the Second and Third Pylons with the Great [[hypostyle|Hypostyle]] Hall: 134 papyrus columns under a stone roof. Ramesses II finished its decoration, added his battle scenes on the south wall, and built a small temple at the east end for people to bring their prayers.

steps.label: Sety II and Ramesses III
steps.text: In front of the Second Pylon, Sety II and Ramesses III built rest stops for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu. In the south-west corner Ramesses III began a temple for Khonsu, the son of Amun and Mut.

steps.label: Shoshenq I
steps.text: Shoshenq I, a king of Libyan descent, closed the area in front of the Second Pylon with a great colonnaded court, swallowing the two boat shrines. On its south-east gate (the Bubastite Portal) he recorded his campaign into Palestine.

steps.label: Taharqo
steps.text: Taharqo, one of the Kushite kings from Nubia, put a giant kiosk of ten papyrus columns in the middle of the court and a building by the Sacred Lake with a deep well, which seems to have been meant to reach the waters of creation thought to flow under the ground.

steps.label: Nectanebo I
steps.text: Nectanebo I, one of the last Egyptian-born kings, built the huge mud-brick wall that still surrounds the precinct, and started the First Pylon, the largest ever begun in Egypt. It was never finished.

steps.label: Philip Arrhidaeus and the Ptolemies
steps.text: The Macedonian and Greek kings kept the temple going in Egyptian style. A granite shrine in the name of Philip Arrhidaeus, half-brother of Alexander the Great, replaced Thutmose III’s at the centre. Ptolemy III gave the Khonsu temple its tall gate (Bab el-Amara), and the temple of Opet was finished next to it.

mk-temple.name: Senusret I’s temple
mk-temple.today: Almost nothing left: a few granite door sills and a calcite stand in an empty square, the “Middle Kingdom court”.

white-chapel.name: White Chapel
white-chapel.today: Taken apart by Amenhotep III and packed into the Third Pylon. Rebuilt in the Open Air Museum. Its original position is uncertain; the plan shows a guess.

am1-gate.name: Amenhotep I’s west gateway
am1-gate.today: Gone: removed for Thutmose I’s Fourth Pylon.

am1-shrine.name: Amenhotep I’s calcite boat shrine
am1-shrine.today: Moved, later reused in the Third Pylon; rebuilt in the Open Air Museum. Its exact first position is disputed.

am1-chapels.name: Amenhotep I’s chapels
am1-chapels.today: Replaced in sandstone by Thutmose III.

pylon4.name: Fourth Pylon
pylon4.today: Standing, in ruins. With the Fifth Pylon, the oldest part of the temple still standing in place.

wadjet.name: Hall between the Fourth and Fifth Pylons (Wadjet Hall)
wadjet.today: Ruined; many of Thutmose I’s Osiris statues still line it.

th1-walls.name: Thutmose I’s stone walls round the core

th1-obelisks.name: Obelisks of Thutmose I
th1-obelisks.today: One still stands, between the Third and Fourth Pylons.

th2-pylon.name: Pylon of Thutmose II and his festival court
th2-pylon.today: Gone: pulled down by Amenhotep III. Its blocks were found inside the Third Pylon.

th2-obelisks.name: Obelisks of Thutmose II (raised by Hatshepsut)
th2-obelisks.today: Gone: their bases were later covered by the Third Pylon.

hat-obelisks.name: Hatshepsut’s obelisks in the Wadjet Hall
hat-obelisks.today: The northern one still stands; part of the other lies near the Sacred Lake.

hat-palace.name: Hatshepsut’s sanctuary rooms (“Palace of Maat”)
hat-palace.today: Partly preserved round the later granite shrine; her images there were later destroyed.

red-chapel.name: Red Chapel
red-chapel.today: Taken down by Thutmose III; blocks later reused in the Third Pylon. Rebuilt in the Open Air Museum.

pylon8.name: Eighth Pylon
pylon8.today: Standing, with decoration changed by later kings.

akhmenu.name: Akhmenu, the festival temple of Thutmose III
akhmenu.today: Standing, partly roofless. Its tent-pole columns are unique.

contra.name: Contra-temple (east)
contra.today: Ruined. A place where people outside could approach the god.

th3-shrine.name: Thutmose III’s granite boat shrine
th3-shrine.today: Replaced in the name of Philip Arrhidaeus.

pylon7.name: Seventh Pylon
pylon7.today: Standing. North of it is the Cachette Court, where hundreds of buried statues were found in 1903.

pylon3.name: Third Pylon
pylon3.today: Standing, ruined. Emptied by 20th-century archaeologists, it gave back the White Chapel, the Red Chapel blocks and other buildings.

pylon10.name: Tenth Pylon
pylon10.today: Standing. Begun by Amenhotep III, finished by Horemheb.

gem-pa-aten.name: Gem-pa-Aten, Akhenaten’s temple to the Aten
gem-pa-aten.today: Gone: dismantled by Horemheb. Its blocks (talatat) were found inside the Second, Ninth and Tenth Pylons.

pylon2.name: Second Pylon
pylon2.today: Standing; now the west end of the Great Hypostyle Hall.

pylon9.name: Ninth Pylon
pylon9.today: Standing. Thousands of Akhenaten’s talatat were found inside it.

hypostyle.name: Great Hypostyle Hall
hypostyle.today: Standing; most of the roof has fallen.

r2-east.name: Ramesses II’s eastern temple (“Amun who hears prayers”)

great-court.name: Great Court (Shoshenq I)
great-court.today: Standing: the first space you enter.

pylon1.name: First Pylon
pylon1.today: Standing, unfinished; remains of mud-brick building ramps still lean against it.

philip-shrine.name: Granite boat shrine of Philip Arrhidaeus
philip-shrine.today: Standing, at the centre of the temple.

timeline.intro: Karnak was built, pulled down and rebuilt for about 2,000 years. Almost every building was paid for by a king, and carries his name. Tap a period to see who built what.

periods.label: Before
periods.text: Thebes was a small provincial town. When the Intef family of Thebes fought for the throne, around 2100 BC, they built a small temple for Amun-Ra here. It is known only from a few stones.

periods.label: Middle Kingdom
periods.text: The Theban kings reunited Egypt. Senusret I built Amun a proper stone temple.

periods.label: War with the Hyksos
periods.text: The country split again; foreign rulers, the Hyksos, held the north. Theban kings fought them for over thirty years and won under Ahmose. Amun got the credit.

periods.label: New Kingdom
periods.text: Egypt’s empire years. Wealth from wars in Nubia and the Near East poured into Amun’s temple, and almost every king added to it. Most of what you see today dates from now.

periods.label: Divided kingdom
periods.text: Egypt broke into parts. High priests of Amun ruled the south from Thebes; Libyan and later Kushite kings built when they could.

periods.label: Late Period
periods.text: Kings ruled from the north and built little at Karnak, until Nectanebo I’s huge wall and gateway.

periods.label: Greek kings
periods.text: After Alexander the Great, Macedonian and Greek kings ruled as pharaohs and kept building in Egyptian style.

periods.label: Roman Egypt
periods.text: Tourists came to look. The temple faded; in AD 356 the emperor ordered pagan temples closed, and churches were built among the ruins.

gods.intro: Karnak belonged to one god above all: Amun, “the Hidden One”. With his wife Mut and their son Khonsu he made up the [[theban-triad|Theban Triad]], the divine family of Thebes. Why these three, and why here?

rise.heading: How a local god became king of the gods

steps.label: A local god
steps.text: Amun was a fairly obscure god before the Middle Kingdom, worshipped at Thebes, then a provincial town.

steps.label: The Theban kings win
steps.text: The Intef family of Thebes fought their way to rule all Egypt. Their god had led them to victory, and their successors gave him a stone temple.

steps.label: The second victory
steps.text: Theban kings drove out the Hyksos and reunited Egypt again. Amun’s reputation, and his temple, grew with every victory.

steps.label: Amun-Ra, King of the Gods
steps.text: Amun was joined with the old sun god Ra of Heliopolis as Amun-Ra, “King of the Gods”. Kings went to Karnak to have their choice confirmed by him, and spent the wealth of their wars on his house.

steps.label: The break
steps.text: Akhenaten turned against Amun, cut out his name and closed his temple. It lasted a few years. Afterwards Amun’s figures were carved back in; you can still spot the repairs.

steps.label: God as ruler
steps.text: When Egypt split, Amun himself was treated as the supreme authority. Decisions were put to him through oracles at Karnak.

family.heading: Why a family of three?
text: Egyptian priests often grouped gods into families of three: father, mother, child. Each big city had one. At Thebes it was Amun, Mut and Khonsu, and each had a home: Amun’s temple at the centre, Mut’s precinct to the south, Khonsu’s temple at the south-west.

The family moved between their houses. At festivals their statues travelled in portable boats along sphinx avenues, by water to Luxor Temple, and across the Nile to the temples on the west bank. The boat shrines of Sety II and Ramesses III in the Great Court each have three rooms: one for each member of the family.
Thebes had other gods too. Montu, a war god, has his own precinct just north of the wall. It is closed to visitors.

building.intro: No cranes, and for most of its history no iron tools. Karnak was built with copper and bronze chisels, stone hammers, ropes, sledges, boats and mud-brick ramps, and the evidence is still on site.

sections.heading: Where the stone came from
text: Most of Karnak is sandstone from Gebel el-Silsila, about 160 km upriver. Granite for obelisks, door frames and colossal statues came from Aswan, further south still. Fine limestone came from Tura near Cairo, calcite (“Egyptian alabaster”) from Hatnub, and red quartzite from Gebel Ahmar. Everything heavy travelled by boat.
The early temple was limestone. It did not survive the yearly wetting and drying of the flood plain, so from Thutmose III on, builders switched to sandstone.

citations.locator: Materials; Quarrying and dressing blocks; Change in techniques and materials over time

sections.heading: How a pylon went up
text: Foundations were trenches partly filled with clean sand, which spreads the load. Blocks arrived roughly cut and were fitted on site, each course to its neighbours. As the walls grew, workers built mud-brick ramps against them, raising the ramps about a metre at a time. Only the outer faces were smoothed, once the wall was complete; the core was often rubble or old blocks.
The First Pylon was never finished, so it still shows all of this: remains of the ramps on its inner side, smoothed and rough blocks side by side, and a moulding only roughed out.

citations.locator: Foundations; Building techniques; Pylons, gateways and doors

sections.heading: Columns and roofs
text: Columns were stacks of stone drums. Plumb lines kept them straight, and the papyrus flowers and buds were carved after the stones were in place: on some columns the capital starts in the middle of a block. Then everything was smoothed and painted.

Stone beams could only span so far. The biggest gaps bridged in stone at Karnak are about 7 metres; anything wider needed wood. In the Hypostyle Hall the roof slabs are 9 m long and over a metre thick, and some architraves are made of up to four blocks stacked together.

citations.locator: Column construction; Roofing

sections.heading: Obelisks
text: An [[obelisk]] is a single piece of granite. At Aswan, quarrymen pounded trenches round it with balls of hard dolerite stone up to 30 cm across. The unfinished obelisk still lying there shows the marks. Thutmose I’s obelisks weigh about 143 tonnes each; Hatshepsut’s about 323.

The stone was dragged on a sledge to the river, floated down on a barge and dragged again to the temple. Nobody knows for sure how it was stood up. One idea: it was slid down a ramp into a sand-filled pit over its base, and tipped upright as the sand was removed. Another: it was levered up on its base, using a groove cut into the pedestal.

citations.locator: Quarrying and dressing blocks; Obelisks: transport and erection

sections.heading: Old temples inside new ones
text: [[pylon|Pylons]] have a casing of good stone and a filled core, and kings filled them with whatever was in the way. Amenhotep III packed the Third Pylon with the chapels he cleared to build it, among them Senusret I’s White Chapel and Hatshepsut’s Red Chapel. Horemheb filled three pylons with Akhenaten’s temples, on purpose, to wipe them out.
That is why Karnak has an Open Air Museum: modern archaeologists took those blocks back out and rebuilt the chapels. Tens of thousands of Akhenaten’s talatat blocks are still being studied.

citations.locator: Reuse of building materials
Amenhotep III; Horemheb

sections.heading: The wavy wall
text: The great mud-brick wall around the precinct is up to 12 m thick. It was built in sections, with the brick courses of neighbouring sections laid on slightly curved beds, and reeds and timber beams laid in for strength. The result is a wall whose courses rise and fall like waves. The Egyptians may have seen in it the waters of creation round the god’s island.

citations.locator: Enclosure walls
Measurements of the Nectanebo I wall

thebes.intro: Karnak was the largest of many temples in ancient Thebes, a city spread over both banks of the Nile. Its ancient name was Ipet-isut, “the most select of places”.
text: On the east bank stood the great temples of the gods. Karnak itself is four precincts: Amun-Ra in the centre (where you are), Mut to the south, Montu to the north, and Akhenaten’s demolished Aten temples to the east. Only the Amun precinct is open to visitors.

A processional road lined with about 700 sphinxes runs about 2 km south to Luxor Temple. On the west bank, kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings and worshipped in their memorial temples along the edge of the desert.
The Nile used to run much closer. As it slowly moved west, the kings followed it, building new quays and gateways further out. That is one reason Karnak grew westward, gate by gate.

life.intro: Karnak was not a monument. It was the house of a god, with a household: priests, scribes, bakers, butchers, store-keepers, and fields across Egypt to pay for it all.

ritual.heading: Every morning
steps: At dawn a purified priest entered the dark sanctuary, lit a torch and burned incense.
He broke the clay seal on the shrine, drew back the bolt and opened the doors to see the god’s face.
He knelt, kissed the ground and sang hymns of praise.
He took out the statue, cleaned it, dressed it in fresh linen, oils and make-up, and put it back.
He offered food and drink, then closed and sealed the shrine again.
He walked out backwards, sweeping away his footprints. The food was then shared among the temple staff.
ritual.note: In theory the king did all this, and the walls always show him doing it. In practice the high priest of Amun stood in for him. The statue itself, though shown life-size on the walls, was probably small: gold, silver and precious wood, a little over 30 cm tall.

citations.locator: Introduction to the Daily Ritual; discussion of the shrine and statue

festivals.heading: Festival days
text: A few times a year the god came out. Priests carried his statue in a portable boat shrine (a [[bark]]) on their shoulders, and people lined the route. The biggest outing was the Opet Festival, when Amun travelled to Luxor Temple. In the Valley Festival he crossed the river to visit the temples of dead kings on the west bank.

For most people this was as close as they got to the god. Others brought their prayers to the back of the temple, where small temples like Thutmose III’s contra-temple and Ramesses II’s eastern temple let them approach without going in.

estate.heading: The god’s estate
text: Around the temple were storehouses, bakeries, workshops, animal pens, aviaries for sacred geese and the priests’ houses. The temple owned land and collected taxes far beyond Thebes; it brought in great wealth.

citations.locator: Temple function: estate, storehouses, land and taxation

after.intro: The temple outlived the pharaohs by centuries, was nearly forgotten, and was then rediscovered, quarried, recorded and rebuilt. The Karnak you visit is partly the work of the last 130 years.

events.text: Greek and Roman tourists came to marvel at the Hypostyle Hall and scratched their names on the walls.
Emperor Constantius II ordered pagan temples closed. Karnak was already largely abandoned; Christians built churches among the ruins, and painted saints can still be seen in the Akhmenu.
Centuries of near silence: only one medieval traveller is known to have written about the ruins.
An Italian traveller describes the ruins at Luxor, the first European record.
Napoleon’s scholars draw Karnak for the Description de l’Égypte.
Champollion deciphers hieroglyphs; he and Lepsius copy the inscriptions. Local people are still quarrying the ruins for stone.
A permanent works service is set up at Karnak under Georges Legrain.
On 3 October eleven columns of the Hypostyle Hall collapse. Legrain rebuilds them.
In the court north of the Seventh Pylon, Legrain finds a pit with about 800 statues and 17,000 bronzes, buried in ancient times: the Karnak Cachette.
Henri Chevrier finishes rebuilding the Hall, clears the Sacred Lake and continues work on the pylons.
The Franco-Egyptian Centre (CFEETK) takes over the study and conservation of the temple; it rebuilds the Red Chapel in the Open Air Museum.
Work goes on: the avenue of sphinxes to Luxor has been uncovered, and walls, reliefs and columns are still being recorded.

rituals.title: Rituals and festivals
rituals.intro: Karnak ran on a timetable. The god was served every day, honoured on set days of the month, and taken out in procession on the great festivals of the year. Once in a long reign the king also renewed his own power. Many of these rites are carved on the temple’s walls, so you can still find them.

rhythms.label: Every day
rhythms.text: Three services: a long one at dawn, shorter ones in the afternoon and evening.

rhythms.label: Every month
rhythms.text: Feasts tied to the moon, and a ten-day visit by Amun of Luxor to the west bank.

rhythms.label: Every year
rhythms.text: The great festivals: Opet, the Valley Festival, Osiris in Khoiak, the New Year.

rhythms.label: Once in a reign
rhythms.text: The jubilee (heb-sed), after 30 years on the throne.

daily.heading: Every day
text: The main service took place every morning, after first light. Similar but shorter rites followed in the afternoon and in the evening. Step through the morning service below.

services.label: Morning service
services.text: The shrine is opened, the statue is cleaned, dressed and fed.

daily.after: When the god had eaten, the food was taken away with its own ceremony, the “reversion of offerings”, and shared among the temple staff.

citations.locator: Frequency; sequence of the morning ritual; reversion of offerings (episodes 34–40)

purity.heading: Making the priests pure
purity.intro: One of the Egyptian words for priest carries the idea of purity. A priest’s body had to be made pure before he could enter the temple, and kept pure for as long as he served.

groups.label: Before a month of duty
items: No sex for several days before service began, and none during it.

Days of “drinking natron”, a natural salt. A complaint from the temple of Khnum at Elephantine, written under Ramesses IV and V, accuses a priest of going under the god’s carrying poles after only seven days of natron, with three days still to go.

citations.locator: Purity: abstinence before and during service
Verso, lines 9–11: “7 days of drinking natron”; “3 days of drinking natron” still due

groups.label: Every day on duty
items: Shave the whole body. Herodotus says priests did this every other day, so that no lice could live on them while they served the gods.
Bathe in cold water: twice by day and twice by night in Herodotus’s time. In the Ramesside period the rule was three baths a day in the temple’s sacred lake.
Rinse the mouth with natron dissolved in water.
Wear fresh white linen and sandals of papyrus, nothing else. Wool was not allowed in the temple.

citations.locator: Histories 2.37.2–3: shaving, linen and papyrus sandals, cold baths
Purity: three baths a day in the Ramesside period; natron mouth-rinse; no wool

groups.label: Always
items: Keep the food taboos. They differed from region to region: fish was forbidden in one province, honey in another. Herodotus adds that priests could not bear even to look at beans.

citations.locator: Purity: circumcision; regional food taboos (Third and Sixth Upper Egyptian nomes)

purity.oil: Oils mostly belonged to the god: the statue was anointed in the morning service. In scenes of the king acting as chief priest, he was washed, dressed and anointed in the “House of the Morning” before entering the temple. Which oils, if any, ordinary priests put on is not recorded in the sources used for this guide.

oilCitations.locator: p. 46: priests “drinking” natron before their course; the king-priest robed and anointed; the House of the Morning

purity.note: Most of these details come from Herodotus, a Greek visitor of the 5th century BC, and from later texts. The rules changed over time and from temple to temple.
purity.lake: At Karnak the water came from the Sacred Lake, south of the temple.
purity.wall: The same idea on a wall: on the west side of the Hall, Horus and Seth pour streams of life signs over Sety I.

women.heading: Women in the temple
women.intro: Women did serve the gods at Karnak. Herodotus wrote that no woman could be a priest, but Egyptian titles, coffins and wall scenes show otherwise.

roles.name: God’s Wife of Amun
roles.text: The highest-ranking priestess of Amun. Queen Ahmose-Nefertari was the first royal woman to hold the office, recorded on a stela in the temple of Amun at Karnak. Scenes show the God’s Wife purified in the sacred lake and following the king into the sanctuary. In the 8th to 6th centuries BC the office went to unmarried king’s daughters, who built chapels of their own, mostly at Karnak.

citations.locator: Stela at Karnak; scenes of purification in the sacred lake and entering the sanctuary
Label: a celibate high priestess; relief from a chapel in North Karnak
Chapels of the God’s Wives, mostly at Karnak; shown making herself pure to enter the temple

roles.name: Singers of Amun
roles.text: The most common role. Women with the title “chantress” or “singer” of Amun sang hymns during rituals and festivals, shaking a sistrum, a metal rattle. The coffin of Meresamun, around 800 BC, calls her “Singer in the Interior of the Temple of Amun at Karnak”: in her time women sang inside the temple, while men played instruments in the rituals outside.

citations.locator: Meresamun’s coffin title; women singers inside, men instrumentalists outside; sistrum

roles.name: Musicians and dancers
roles.text: Festivals had music and dance. Blocks from Hatshepsut’s Red Chapel show acrobatic dancers and harpists in festival scenes.

monthly.heading: Every month and every ten days
text: The temple also kept feasts tied to the moon. Next to the daily-ritual scenes in the Hypostyle Hall, Sety I is shown at the feasts of the first and the sixth day of the month.

Every ten days, from the New Kingdom on, the Amun of Luxor Temple crossed the Nile to the small temple at Medinet Habu, where the primeval gods were believed to be buried. This is called the Decade festival.

year.heading: Every year: the festival calendar
year.intro: The Egyptian year had three seasons of four months: the flood (Akhet), the growing season (Peret) and the harvest (Shemu). Every month had 30 days, and five extra days closed the year. Because there was no leap year, this calendar slowly drifted against the real seasons.

festivals.name: New Year
festivals.text: The first day of the year. On the east wall of the Hypostyle Hall, Sety I is shown at the New Year festival.

festivals.name: Festivals of Mut
festivals.text: Mut had her own festivals. Hatshepsut built a “columned portico of drunkenness” at Mut’s temple, where a festival of drunkenness was held, reportedly in the first month of the year. The Hall also shows Sety I at a festival of Mut.

festivals.name: Opet Festival
festivals.when: 2nd month of the flood, 11 to 27 days
festivals.text: Amun, Mut and Khonsu travelled to Luxor Temple, and the king renewed his kingship there. Under Thutmose III it lasted 11 days; by Ramesses III, 24 days or more.

citations.locator: The Opet Festival
Dates and duration

festivals.name: Osiris in Khoiak
festivals.text: As the flood went down, priests shaped earth into figures of Osiris, sowed them with grain and watered them until they sprouted: the god coming back to life. At Karnak the rites ran from day 18 to 26, with a procession of Osiris on day 26. The galleries where such figures were buried survive at Karnak.

festivals.name: Valley Festival
festivals.when: 2nd month of the harvest, at the new moon
festivals.text: Amun crossed the river to visit the temples on the west bank, and families feasted at the tombs of their relatives.

jubilee.heading: Once in a reign: the jubilee
text: The heb-sed was a royal jubilee, celebrated after 30 years of rule and repeated every three years after that. It renewed the king’s strength.

At Karnak, Senusret I’s White Chapel was decorated for his jubilee, and Hatshepsut raised her granite obelisks for a jubilee in year 16 of her reign. On the walls, gods promise kings “millions of jubilees”.

processions.heading: Processions
text: On festival days the god left the sanctuary. His statue stayed hidden inside a small shrine on a portable boat, the [[bark|bark]], carried on poles by priests. Along the way the bearers rested the bark in small shrines, the bark stations.

Under Hatshepsut the Opet procession went to Luxor on foot, stopping at six bark stations, and came back by river. By the Ramesside period each god, and the king, had a bark of his own, and the journey south went upstream by boat.
